facts.claim: "This Is Life" is a single by Los Angeles trio Winnetka Bowling League featuring Medium Build and Dawes, released June 27, 2024, and it runs about 3 minutes 32 seconds.
The song is credited to Matthew Koma, Taylor Goldsmith and Nicholas Carpenter (Medium Build) as writers.

Koma already had a verse and chorus when he met Medium Build's Nick. Nick spotted a Dawes poster in Koma's studio and said Dawes was his favorite band. Koma then invited him to meet the Dawes members at a Christmas show he was playing the next night.
Koma says the song started when a viral TikTok song, 'Rectangular', led him to Medium Build's videos. He then sent Taylor Goldsmith some of Medium Build's music.

Medium Build (Nick Carpenter) said Koma sent him the song and told him he and Taylor would write on it. He also said he didn't believe Koma was friends with Dawes' Taylor until Koma got him free Dawes tickets.
Koma describes the single as a creative spark and a preview of where the band is headed. He calls it a one-off single featuring Dawes' Taylor Goldsmith and Medium Build's Nick Carpenter.
An acoustic version followed. Koma described the collaborators as 'a bunch of sloppy dudes laughing and giddy about singin' in a truck'.
A deluxe edition of the single was later issued with the original, a live version and an acoustic version.

The single followed the band's debut album Sha La La, released in May 2024 on Local Weather/MDDN Records. The album is described as a back-to-basics record about Koma rediscovering what he loves about music.

Winnetka Bowling League is the project of Matthew Koma. He premiered it in 2018 with 'On the 5' via RCA Records. He had earlier produced tracks on Shania Twain's album Now, including 'Life's About to Get Good'.
Winnetka Bowling League performed the song with Medium Build at the Ryman in Nashville on Nov. 10, 2024, while supporting Dawes on tour. Koma told the crowd he had been to forty Dawes concerts.

research.lineage: The song sits in a nostalgic, confessional indie-pop/alt-rock songwriter tradition that Koma ties to his fandom of Dawes and Taylor Goldsmith's songwriting, and a Vanderbilt Hustler review called the band 'Modern Gen Z Rock' in contrast to Dawes' 'Modern Dad Rock'.

draft:
The verses of **This Is Life** read like a junk drawer emptied onto a table: mall-store cologne, drinking in chain-restaurant parking lots, a Brand New singalong from back before the singer got caught, Montauk summers before the money moved in. Nothing gets ranked. Being broke enough to do degrading things for cash sits right next to hearing from more famous people that you've made it. Then comes the line about parents that hurts most. Once they were security blankets. Now they're wrinkled and racist. The song lets love and disappointment share that single verse and doesn't pick one.

That refusal to sort is the feeling. "Friends from home like old ghosts from past lives" names a kind of grief that isn't quite grief. Nobody died. People just drifted into other versions of themselves. The chorus answers all of it with three words repeated until they stop sounding like a shrug and start sounding like acceptance. To be honest, nine straight "this is life"s can feel thin on the page. Sung, the repetition does what it should. The stacked voices put a main melody under a higher harmony, and the effect is less a hook than a group of people agreeing.

The music stays out of the way of all that confession. A strummed acoustic guitar and a walking bass line carry it at a relaxed, steady medium tempo. The drums keep it simple with kick, snare and hi-hat, and a synth pad holds the chords underneath. The production is clean and polished. The lead voice is clear and a little breathy, so lines about Craigslist and cosmic weed epiphanies land without any wink.

The song was written by Winnetka Bowling League's Matthew Koma with Medium Build's Nick Carpenter and Dawes' Taylor Goldsmith, and it grew out of fandom. Koma found Medium Build through a viral TikTok song and sent the music to Goldsmith. Carpenter noticed a Dawes poster in Koma's studio and said Dawes was his favorite band, and Koma invited him to meet them the next night. Carpenter admitted he didn't believe Koma knew Goldsmith until the free tickets showed up. Koma has been to forty Dawes concerts. So when the bridge declares "Taylor says that we're all gonna die," it plays like a joke among friends, which is exactly what the song says God is: "I think God's a dog out the window," laughing at something only the people in the car understand. Koma called the acoustic version's crew "a bunch of sloppy dudes laughing and giddy," and that giddiness is all over the original too, set against the steady bass.

It takes the most embarrassing, tender and ugly pieces of your past and has a room full of friends sing them back to you as if they were simply the shape of being alive.
